$comment: Employment policy set — generated when the company plans to hire within 12 months. The California-conditioned clauses are the spec's own §2.1 example (meal break, rest period, PTO accrual).

clauses.title: At-Will Employment
clauses.rationale: At-will status is the default everywhere in this library except by contract, but it is eroded by handbook language promising process. Saying it plainly, and limiting who can change it, is the protection.
clauses.body: Employment with the Company is [[at-will employment|at-will employment]] and may be terminated by either party at any time, with or without cause or notice. No manager, and no statement in any handbook or policy, alters this status except in a writing signed by the {{principalTitle}}.

clauses.title: Classification
clauses.rationale: Misclassification is the most common and most expensive wage-and-hour error, and it is decided by duties and salary rather than by job title.
clauses.body: Each employee shall be classified as [[exempt employee|exempt employee]] or non-exempt based on their actual duties and compensation, not on job title. Classification shall be documented at hire and reviewed whenever duties change materially. Non-exempt employees shall record all hours worked.

clauses.title: Work Authorization
clauses.rationale: Form I-9 must be completed within three business days of the first day of work. The penalty attaches to the paperwork failure itself, independent of anyone's actual status.
clauses.body: The Company shall complete Form I-9 for every employee within three (3) business days of their first day of work, retain the forms separately from personnel files, and apply the same documentary requirements to all employees without regard to national origin or citizenship status.
defects: The clause's citation (8 U.S.C. section 1324a only) does not name section 1324b, which is the actual statutory source of the documentary-uniformity claim. Whether this is worth flagging as a citation gap depends on whether a reader would understand '8 U.S.C. section 1324a' to cover the whole clause or just the verification-duty sentence -- not resolved here, but noted because this project's stated failure pattern is exactly 'the clause reproduces something true and cites the wrong or incomplete provision.'

Robison's discrimination-requirement holding was for the pre-1996 version of section 1324b(a)(6); the opinion states the 1996 amendment made the discrimination requirement express rather than changing it, and the court read the requirement into the earlier text too -- so the current text should hold a fortiori, but the current (post-1996) statutory text was not independently fetched to confirm the amendment reads the way the opinion describes it, since every host carrying it directly is blocked.

clauses.title: Written Offer Requirements
clauses.rationale: Several states require a written wage notice at hire. A standard offer template satisfies that and prevents inconsistent side promises.
clauses.body: Every offer shall be made in writing and shall state the position, the rate and basis of pay, the pay schedule, the classification determined under <<xr:emp_classification>>, and any conditions of employment. Verbal assurances about job security or future compensation are not authorized.

clauses.title: Independent Contractor Classification
clauses.benchmark: Present in 58% of employment policy sets
clauses.rationale: California's ABC test in particular makes most contractors employees. The exposure is back wages, taxes, and penalties across the whole engagement.
clauses.body: Before engaging any individual as an independent contractor, the Company shall evaluate the engagement under the test applicable in {{opStateLong}} and document the analysis. Contractors shall not be given Company email, fixed schedules, or supervision of employees, and shall sign an agreement assigning intellectual property to the Company.

clauses.title: Overtime
clauses.rationale: Federal overtime is weekly; several states add a daily threshold. Paying on the federal rule alone underpays in those states.
clauses.body: Non-exempt employees shall receive overtime at one and one-half times the regular rate for hours worked over forty (40) in a workweek, and at any additional rate required by the law of {{opStateLong}}. Overtime must be paid whether or not it was authorized in advance.

sources.title: CourtListener — Forrester v. Roth's I.G.A. Foodliner, Inc. (9th Cir. 1981) 646 F.2d 413
CourtListener — Chao v. Gotham Registry, Inc. (2d Cir. 2008) 514 F.3d 280

defects: The clause states the payment duty as unconditional ('must be paid whether or not it was authorized in advance') with no mention of the employer's-knowledge condition both circuits treat as load-bearing. In the ordinary case an employer that requires advance authorization also has visibility into hours worked (timekeeping, direct supervision), so the condition is usually satisfied and the clause's practical guidance is not wrong for the case it is written for. The gap matters at the edge: an employee who conceals hours or bypasses the time-reporting system entirely, then claims unreported overtime after the fact, is exactly the Forrester fact pattern, and on those facts the employer may owe nothing. The clause gives the reader no way to tell the ordinary case from the edge case.

29 U.S.C. section 207 and section 203(g) were not independently fetched -- every host that would carry them was blocked. The quoted statutory language above is the courts' own quotation of the text, not a primary read of the Office of the Law Revision Counsel's version.
The clause's second half ('and at any additional rate required by the law of {{opStateLong}}') is a pure deferral and was not checked -- it names no state-specific rule to verify.

ea_overtime (employment-agreement) makes close to the same two claims in worker-facing language and was not separately checked. Its risk profile is different -- it faces the employee being offered the job, not an internal handbook policy -- and it deserves its own pass rather than being assumed covered by this one.

clauses.title: Employee Invention Assignment
clauses.rationale: Founder IP assignment does not cover employees. Every hire needs their own assignment signed before the first day of work.
clauses.body: Every employee shall sign an invention assignment and confidentiality agreement before their first day of work, assigning to the Company all inventions and works created in the scope of employment, and including any statutory carve-out required in {{opStateLong}}. An assignment signed after work has begun may require separate consideration to be enforceable.

sources.title: CourtListener — Lake Land Employment Group of Akron, LLC v. Columber (Ohio 2004) 101 Ohio St.3d 242
CourtListener — Labriola v. Pollard Group, Inc. (Wash. 2004) 100 P.3d 791

defects: Both opinions read address noncompetition covenants specifically, not a bare invention-assignment-and-confidentiality agreement with no competitive restriction. The general contract-law question is the same ('is a promise made after an at-will relationship already exists supported by consideration'), and nothing found suggests courts draw a different line for invention assignments -- but that was not independently confirmed with a case actually presenting an invention-assignment fact pattern, only inferred from the shared underlying doctrine.

This confirms a split exists; it does not tell a reader which side any particular {{opStateLong}} falls on, and the clause does not either -- by design, since this is the jurisdiction-neutral corpus and state-specific answers were parked. A reader who wants to know whether separate consideration is actually required in their state still has to look it up themselves.

Both sources are on the same host (courtlistener.com), so this does not meet this project's two-independent-host standard even though it draws on two independent courts reaching opposite conclusions -- an artifact of how host-independence is measured here, not a weakness in the finding itself.

clauses.title: Anti-Harassment Policy and Training
clauses.rationale: A published policy with a real reporting path is the first element of the employer's defense, and training is mandatory at low headcount in several states.
clauses.body: The Company shall maintain a written anti-harassment and anti-retaliation policy with at least two reporting channels, at least one of which does not run through the employee’s direct manager. The Company shall provide the training required by {{opStateLong}} at the intervals and headcount thresholds that law specifies.

clauses.title: Confidentiality
clauses.benchmark: Present in 88% of employee policy sets
clauses.rationale: A confidentiality obligation without the whistleblower carve-out can itself be unlawful, so the two belong in the same clause.
clauses.body: Employees shall not use or disclose Company confidential information during or after employment, except as required by law. Nothing in this policy prohibits an employee from reporting a suspected violation of law to a government agency, participating in an agency investigation, or discussing wages and working conditions with coworkers.

clauses.title: Arbitration of Employment Disputes
clauses.benchmark: Present in 41% of employment policy sets
clauses.rationale: Genuinely two-sided. Arbitration limits class exposure but is unenforceable for some claims, cannot be a condition of employment in some states, and shifts the fee burden to the employer.
clauses.body: If the Company adopts arbitration, the agreement shall be a separate signed document rather than a handbook provision, shall be mutual, shall require the Company to bear arbitration costs beyond a court filing fee, and shall carve out claims that cannot lawfully be compelled to arbitration in {{opStateLong}}, including sexual harassment and assault claims under federal law.
